deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation. It is a printed page, p. xi of the historical preface (Vorrede) of a German textbook of arithmetic and algebra. The shelf mark 'HB.Leiste' points to Gauss's Handbibliothek copy of Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, 1790). The type is Fraktur with Antiqua for Latin and Italian titles, and there are no visible handwritten annotations by Gauss.

The text continues a survey of the history of mathematics:
- (14th century) Maximus Planudes was the first among the Greeks to use the Indian/Arabic numerals. Leibniz praised the Englishman Richard Suisset (Swineshead, 'the Calculator').
- (15th century) The greatest scholars were Germans:
  - Nicholas of Cusa (died 1464), a forerunner of Copernicus.
  - Georg von Peurbach (died 1461), whose arithmetic Melanchthon edited.
  - Peurbach's pupil Johann Müller (Regiomontanus). He translated Greek mathematical classics, joined algebra with geometry, introduced decimal reckoning into astronomical tables and worked on calendar reform. He also improved printing through Walther's press in Nuremberg and built a legendary iron fly, presumably magnetically guided. He is said to have died in 1475 in his 41st year.
- Among foreigners the text names Leonardo of Pisa and Luca Pacioli. Of Pacioli it cites the Summa ('Arithmetica Geometria Proportioni e Proportionalità', Venice 1494) and 'Divina Proportione' (Venice 1509), saying these are usually taken as the first algebra brought from Arabia to Europe. Pacioli used Leonardo's work.
- The terminology section reports that Pacioli calls the regula falsi by the Arabic name 'Helcataim' (al-khata'ayn, double false position). He calls algebra 'l'Arte maggiore' or 'Divina Proportione'; others call it 'Regola di Cosa' or, in Arabic, 'Algebra u Almucabalah'. The next page explains this as restoration and opposition (al-jabr wa'l-muqabala).

Nothing is computed, so there is nothing to reconstruct mathematically.
errors: Regiomontanus (born 6 June 1436) died in July 1476, not 1475; he died aged 40.
Leonardo of Pisa (Liber Abaci 1202) belongs to the 13th century. The text lists him among 15th-century foreigners; 'nach ihm' partly mitigates this, but the placement is misleading.
'Divina Proportione' (1509) is a treatise on the golden section and proportion, not an algebra. The algebra ('l'arte maggiore', 'regola de la cosa') is in the Summa of 1494.
Pacioli's 1494 work is properly titled 'Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità'. The book abbreviates the title.
The Regiomontanus iron-fly story is a legend; the book itself hedges it with 'vermuthlich' (presumably).

results.what: Historical survey of 14th-15th century mathematicians (Planudes, Swineshead, Cusa, Peurbach, Regiomontanus, Fibonacci, Pacioli) and the etymology of regula falsi / algebra terms
results.usually_credited_to: Christian Leiste (author of the printed textbook), drawing on Kästner/Montucla-style histories

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed page of a standard 18th-century textbook's historical preface in Gauss's library copy. It has no mathematics and no Gauss annotations.

checkable.asserts: Regiomontanus (b. 1436, d. 1476) died aged 40, i.e. in his 41st year; the printed death year 1475 is off by one.
Divina Proportione (1509) appeared 15 years after the Summa (1494).

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription matches the image closely. Hyphenation marks in the image are Fraktur double hyphens '=' ('Kö=nigsberg', 'ge=nannt', 'Geo=metrie', 'astronomi=schen', 'Kalen=ders', 'wer=den', 'Na=men'), rendered as '-' in the transcription.
Page number is printed 'xi' (lowercase roman), consistent with the preceding 'x' and the following 'XII' (as transcribed).
